title: How to review a redesign before it ships
excerpt: Review a redesign against the brief: the phone, the primary action, and words a stranger understands. Taste notes come after those three passes.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. The diagram is the brief a redesign should be checked against.
caption: Review the flow against the goal. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a website design review decide?
faqs.answer: It should decide whether the redesign still does the job in the brief. Check the phone, the primary action, and whether a stranger can say what the company does. A passing review is permission to ship, plus a short list of follow-ups that are too small to be a new phase.

faqs.question: Who needs to be in the review?
faqs.answer: The person who can approve, someone who will use the page, and one reader who did not sit in the design meetings. The outsider's reading is the point of the stranger pass. A room of people who already know the offer will forgive a vague headline.

faqs.question: What if the team dislikes the look but the brief is met?
faqs.answer: Record the preference and ask whether it changes the offer, the action, or the ability to read. If it does not, it can wait for a later pass that has its own time. Restarting layout from taste, the week of launch, is how dates slip.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A website design review checklist is a pass against the brief. Before a redesign ships, the people who asked for it should be able to say whether the page still does the job they wrote down. The offer is recognizable. The primary action is obvious. A stranger can tell what the company does.

Taste will show up in the meeting. Someone will prefer a different typeface, a quieter color, or a photograph from an earlier deck. Those notes help when they point at the brief. They get expensive when they reopen the design because a preference arrived late. The review exists so the room can tell the difference.

## Start from the brief you already agreed

Bring the brief into the room. A useful one is short: who the site is for, the one action it should earn, what must stay, and a few references. If that page is missing, write it in a few sentences before anyone opens the new design. A review without a brief becomes a tour of opinions, and opinions do not have a finish line.

Read the brief out loud. Then open the redesign on a staging URL, not in a slide. The first question is whether the new page still answers the brief. The second is whether anything in the brief was wrong. That second case is a scope change, and it should be named as one. Naming it keeps the launch date attached to a decision someone can see.

On a Hanabi project the brief stays visible through design and build. The review at the end holds the same document against the staging site. If the offer changed during the work, the brief should have changed in writing before this meeting. A surprise offer, revealed as a comment on the hero, is a new project wearing the clothes of a tweak.

## Three passes, in this order

Run the review as three passes. Each pass has a yes or a no. Comments that do not change a yes into a no can wait until the passes are done.

**Mobile.** Open the staging site on the phone the founder actually uses. Read the first screen without pinching. The offer should be visible. The primary action should be tappable. Text should sit in the width of the screen. Sections that were a row on a wide monitor should stack in an order that still makes sense. If the team designed on a large display and only squeezed the layout at the end, this pass is where that shows.

**The primary action.** Name the one thing a new visitor should do. Book a call, buy the product, request a quote, or read the story. Count how many competing actions sit above that one. A second link is fine when it serves a different person, such as an existing customer signing in. A row of equal buttons is a page that has not chosen. The pass fails when a stranger cannot tell which action the company wants.

**Words a stranger understands.** Ask someone who does not work on the product to read the first screen and say what the company does. If they recite a category and miss the offer, the headline is still inside the building. Nielsen Norman Group reported in 2011 that people often leave a web page within 10 to 20 seconds, and that they have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they actually visit. A review that debates the third paragraph while the first sentence is vague is spending its time on words most visitors will never reach. [The Nielsen Norman Group article](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) puts the practical test plainly: to earn a longer visit, the value has to be clear within about 10 seconds.

## What the passes are allowed to reject

Reject a page that hides the offer, breaks the action on a phone, or uses words only the team knows. Reject a page that dropped a path regulars rely on, such as a login, a shop, or a phone number, when the brief said that path stays. Reject a page whose form sends mail nowhere. A polished page that cannot receive a reply is not ready.

Hold comments about taste until the three passes are finished. Then sort them. A note that the type is too light to read is a contrast problem, and it belongs in the pass. A note that someone prefers a serif is a preference. Preferences can be taken when they are cheap and when they do not restart the layout. They should not move the date on their own.

The W3C organizes the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Conformance means meeting the testable success criteria. A pre-launch review can check the part of that bar a team can see in an hour, without claiming a formal audit. Text should be readable against its background. Focus should be visible when you tab through the page. Buttons should have names. The words should still make sense if an image fails to load. Certification is a separate engagement. This meeting is a quality pass the people shipping the site can actually finish.

## How to spend the hour

Give the meeting a shape so it ends.

1. Five minutes on the brief. Read the audience, the action, and the constraints.
2. Fifteen minutes on a phone, with one person sharing the screen and everyone else quiet until the first screen has been described out loud.
3. Fifteen minutes on the primary action, followed through to the confirmation or the calendar.
4. Fifteen minutes on the stranger's reading. One person who was not in the design reviews says what they think the company does.
5. Ten minutes to list the failures as tasks, each with an owner and a done state.

Write the tasks in the project channel before anyone leaves. "Look at the hero" is not a task. "Replace the headline so it names the buyer and the outcome" is a task. "Check mobile" is not a task. "Stack the proof under the offer on a narrow screen and keep the call button visible" is a task.

If a failure means the brief was wrong, stop and rewrite the brief before the tasks multiply. Shipping a redesign against a brief nobody believes is how the next review starts from zero. A changed brief may change the date. Say so in the same note, with the new date next to the new sentence.

Keep a record of what passed. The future argument about whether "we already approved this" is easier when the note lists the three passes and the names of the people who said yes.

## After the yes

A review that passes is a decision to ship, plus a short list of follow-ups that are allowed to happen after launch. Follow-ups are typos, a photograph swap, a sentence in the footer. They are not a new homepage. If the list is long enough to be a phase, it is unfinished scope, and it should be scheduled as scope.

The staging URL should match what will go live. That means the real copy, the forms, the titles in the browser tab, and the links in the navigation. Reviewing a prototype while the real sentences live in a separate document is how surprises survive until the morning after launch. Read the tab title. Send the form to the inbox a customer will reach. Open the page in a private window so you are not looking at a logged-in preview the public will never see.

Once the page is live, the same people need to know how to change it. A passed review still fails the company if nobody can edit the result. The next piece is that handoff: [the handoff that makes a redesign usable after the studio leaves](/blog/redesign-handoff).

If you want a second set of eyes on a redesign before it ships, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the brief. The call should decide fit and whether a proposal is worth writing.
